titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Spell 18, the introduction
work: Book of the Dead of Ani
workEn: Book of the Dead of Ani
draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plate XII. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 72–74; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: The introduction to Spell 18 runs along the upper register of Plate 12 of Ani's papyrus, above the end of Spell 146. In four short sections, each numbered afresh by Budge, two speakers who bear titles of Horus as the son of Osiris, Iun-mut-ef and Sa-mer-ef, present Ani to the tribunals of the gods, and Ani adores Osiris and asks for bread, free going in the realm of the dead and a place among the blessed. Several signs in Budge's print are doubtful, one is unidentified, and a few words are restored.

sentences.i: Said by Iun-mut-ef. He says:
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd in and ḏd·f in red; the name between them is black. This unit opens the introduction to Spell 18, on the upper register of Plate 12, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1 here and at each of the three sections that follow. ḏd in N 'said by N' brings in the speaker: ḏd is the cobra ḏ with the hand d printed under its curve, and in is the reed and water n. The name is a slender column with a pointed top (coded O28, approximate), the pillar iwn, with its stroke; the vulture mwt with t as complement, 'mother'; the horned viper f, 'his'; and a seated figure with pointed headgear as classifier (coded A40, the seated god, approximate; it may be the plain seated man): iwn-mwt-f, 'Pillar of his mother' (Budge: Ān-māut-f). ḏd·f 'he says' is ḏd with the suffix ·f, the sḏm·f. Iun-mut-ef is a title of Horus as the son who upholds his mother, and the title of the priest who plays the son in the rites for the dead; here he presents Ani to the gods.

sentences.l: have-come-(I) · to-you · tribunal · great · who-are-in · heaven · earth · the-necropolis
sentences.i: I have come to you, great tribunal who are in heaven, on earth and in the necropolis.
sentences.n: ii 'come' is the reed-leaf with legs (M18), ii, with a second reed and two strokes as complements and the walking legs as classifier. The speaker's 'I' is not written (Budge supplies it); the form is taken as 'I have come', the stative ii·kwi or the sḏm·n·f ii·n·i with its endings left out. ḫr·tn 'to you' is the placenta ḫ and the mouth r, the preposition ḫr used before persons, with the suffix ·tn 'you' (plural), t and water n with plural strokes; Budge prints ḫr and ·tn as two groups, joined here as one word. ḏꜣḏꜣt 'council, tribunal' is written as in Spell 1: the fire-drill ḏꜣ (coded U28, approximate) twice, a small ring with ears between them (coded W24, not read), t, and a barred T-shaped sign (coded N1, approximate), the seated god and a stroke as classifiers. ꜥꜣt 'great' is the column ꜥꜣ with the arm ꜥ as complement, t and the roll, feminine to agree with ḏꜣḏꜣt. imyw 'who are in' is the sign im with the chick w and a stroke: the plural of the nisba imy, its y not written. pt 'heaven' is the sky sign alone, and tꜣ 'earth' the flat land sign (N16, approximate). ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis', literally 'what is under the god', is the god's flag nṯr with the sign ẖr (T28) and r; Budge's numeral 2 is printed before it. The three realms follow one another without 'and'. A ḏꜣḏꜣt is a court of gods who sit in judgement; Spell 18 proper, from Plate 13, goes through such tribunals one by one.

sentences.i: I have brought you the Osiris Ani.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes n·t with plural strokes; read n·tn 'to you'. Budge prints this and the verb before it as one group; it is divided here. in·n·i 'I have brought' is the sign in (coded W25, approximate: a round-headed sign on two legs) with water n as complement, a second n that marks the sḏm·n·f, and the kneeling man with raised arm for ·i: the past form of ini 'bring'. In the group after it water n stands over t with plural strokes: the n is the preposition 'to', and the suffix ·tn 'you' is written with t and the plural strokes only, its own n not repeated after the preposition's. In the third section the phrase is written in full. wsir 'the Osiris' is a low seat (coded Q2, approximate) over the eye, without the god classifier: the dead man named as an Osiris. ꜣny 'Ani' is the vulture ꜣ, water n with three strokes, two reeds y and the seated man; the two reeds and the man stand in Budge's square brackets and are restored. Iun-mut-ef speaks for Ani, who stands before the gods as a newcomer.

sentences.i: He has done no wrong towards any of the gods.
sentences.n: n 'not' is the arms of negation (D35, approximate) with water n as complement, before the sḏm·f: n sḏm·f, here of the past, 'he has not …'. btꜣ·f is the foot b, t, a small straight-sided cup (coded W10, approximate) that is not read, the vulture ꜣ, the sparrow as classifier of bad things, and ·f: the verb bṯꜣ 'do wrong', written with t for ṯ, as Budge reads it (beta-f). The cup may be a misprinted tethering rope ṯ, the sign the word usually has, but the print does not show one, so the sign stays unread. ḫr 'towards' is the placenta and the mouth, the preposition used of persons. nṯrw 'gods' is the god's flag with a single seated god and a stroke, read as a plural for the sake of nbw 'all', the basket nb with plural strokes. This is the plea at the heart of the judgement of the dead: the one presented has given no god cause for complaint.

sentences.i: Grant that he may be with you every day.
sentences.n: imi 'grant, cause' is the reed i, the owl m written twice and the arm: the imperative of rdi 'give', which with a sḏm·f after it means 'cause that he …'. Budge reads àmmā; the second owl (its body crossed by a forearm in the print) is taken as a complement of m, and the arm, printed as the plain arm, as the classifier of giving. wn·f 'that he may be' is the hare wn with water n as complement and ·f: the sḏm·f of wnn 'be', after imi. ḥnꜥ·tn 'with you' is the twisted wick ḥ, n and the arm ꜥ, with ·tn as before. hrw nb 'every day' is the sun with its stroke, hrw 'day', and the basket nb 'every' after its noun. To be with the gods every day is to share their unending life.

sentences.l: adoring · Osiris · lord · of-Rosetau · (and) · the-Ennead · of-the-gods · great · which-is-in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Adoring Osiris, lord of Rosetau, and the great Ennead of the gods which is in the necropolis.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes dwꜣ in red; the rest is black. A new section begins, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1. dwꜣ 'adoring' is the star dwꜣ with the man with raised arm and the roll as classifiers: the infinitive, used as a heading. wsir is here the eye over the throne with the seated god as classifier: the god himself. nb rꜣ-sṯꜣw 'lord of Rosetau' is the basket nb, then the mouth rꜣ with a stroke, the drag-rope sṯꜣ (V2, approximate), plural strokes and the desert-hill sign, as Rosetau is written in Spell 1. psḏt 'Ennead' is a circle crossed by a bar (X6) with t, and nṯrw 'the gods' is the god's flag three times, the plural: psḏt nṯrw 'the Ennead of the gods'. No 'and' is written before it; it is taken as a second object of dwꜣ. ꜥꜣt 'great' is the column ꜥꜣ, t and the arm (low and flat in the print), feminine to agree with psḏt. imy 'which is in' is the sign im with the sign m (Aa15) as complement and two strokes y, written without the feminine t. ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis' as in the first section. Rosetau is the realm of Sokar in the cemetery of Memphis, where Osiris was said to lie; the Ennead is the company of the nine great gods.

sentences.i: Says the Osiris, the scribe Ani; he says:
sentences.n: The papyrus writes in and ḏd·f in red; the name and title between them are black. in alone before a name is 'says', as in Spell 146: the reed and water n. wsir, the eye over the throne with the seated god, is here 'the Osiris', the dead man named after the god. sš 'scribe' is the scribe's palette with its water-pot and pen (Y3, approximate in the print). ꜣny 'Ani' is spelled as in the first section, and mꜣꜥ-ḫrw 'true of voice' is not written. Budge's numeral 2 follows the name, and ḏd·f 'he says', the cobra and the hand with ·f, stands at the head of line 2. Now Ani speaks for himself.

sentences.i: Hail to you, Foremost of the West, Wennefer who dwells in Abydos!
sentences.n: ind-ḥr·k 'hail to you' is the reed i and the sign nḏ (a staff with a knobbed head, coded Aa27, approximate), then the face ḥr with its stroke and the basket ·k: literally 'greetings to your face'. The cobra ḏ that often follows nḏ is not written. ḫnty 'foremost of' is three jars in a rack (coded W17, approximate), ḫnt, alone; imntt 'the West' is the emblem of the West with t twice and the desert-hill sign. ḫnty imntt 'Foremost of the West' is a title of Osiris. wnn-nfr 'Wennefer', 'he who is perfect', is the hare wn with two waters n and the heart-and-windpipe nfr, with the seated god: a name of Osiris (Budge: Un-nefer). ḥry-ib 'who dwells in' is the face ḥr and the heart ib, each with its stroke. ꜣbḏw 'Abydos' is an ankh-like sign (coded S34, approximate) for ꜣb, the low sign ḏw (N26), the town sign and the foot b, the complement of ꜣb, set last. Abydos was the holy city of Osiris, where his tomb was shown.

sentences.i: I have come to you, my heart bearing truth.
sentences.n: ii is written as in the first section, again without the 'I'. ḫr·k 'to you' is the placenta, the mouth and the basket ·k: Ani speaks to Osiris. ib·i 'my heart' is the heart with its stroke and the seated man ·i. ẖr 'bearing' is the sign ẖr (T28) over the mouth r, its complement: the preposition 'under', used of a load one carries. mꜣꜥt 'truth' is the plinth mꜣꜥ (coded Aa11, approximate), t, and the seated goddess with the feather, Maat herself, as classifier. The clause ib·i ẖr mꜣꜥt has no verb: 'my heart (is) under truth', that is, carries it. The heart is what is weighed against the feather of Maat at the judgement.

sentences.i: There is no wrong in my body.
sentences.n: n before a noun is 'there is no …': the arms of negation (D35, approximate) and water n. isft 'wrong' is the reed i, a tall sign tied round the middle (coded Y1a, approximate), read as the bundle of reeds is that writes isft in Spell 17, the folded cloth s (printed as a tall hairpin) as its complement, the sparrow and the viper f; the sparrow, the classifier of bad things, stands before f, and the t of isft is not written (Budge: àsf). Budge's numeral 3 is printed before the word. m 'in' is the owl. ẖt·i 'my body' is the belly with teats ẖ, t, a stroke and ·i. isft is the disorder that is the opposite of Maat; Ani's body holds none of it.

sentences.i: I have not spoken lies knowingly.
sentences.n: n ḏd 'I have not spoken' is the arms of negation with n, and ḏd, the cobra over the hand lying flat: the n sḏm·f, its 'I' not written (Budge supplies it). grg 'lies' is the pick-like sign grg (U17, approximate) alone. m rḫ 'with knowledge' is the owl m and rḫ, the mouth r and the placenta ḫ with the roll as classifier of abstract things: 'knowingly'. sentences.i: I have not done a deed a second time(?).
sentences.n: n iry·i 'I have not done' is the arms of negation with n, then the eye ir with two reeds y and the seated man ·i; the reeds write a weak ending of the verb and are not translated (Budge: àri-à). sp 'deed, occasion' is the bolt s, the stool p and the threshing floor sp as classifier. The last group is two upright strokes over the pot nw (coded Z4 and W24, approximate): the numeral two, sn, with nw, read as the ordinal snnw 'second' (Budge: sep sen, 'double'). sp snnw is literally 'a second deed', and as a phrase 'a second time': taken here as 'I have not done a deed twice', perhaps 'I have not repeated a wrong'. Budge's 'double' reads the numeral two, not the ordinal that nw makes; the sense is not sure.

sentences.i: May you give me bread and a coming forth into the presence, at the altar of the lords of Maat,
sentences.n: di·k 'may you give' is the arm holding a loaf, di, and the basket ·k: the sḏm·f of rdi 'give', used for a wish. n·i 'to me' is water n and the seated man. t 'bread' is t with a lidded pot (coded W22, approximate), a long loaf (coded X4, approximate) and plural strokes as classifiers (Budge: tau, 'cakes'). pr 'coming forth' is the house pr, the mouth r as complement and the walking legs: the infinitive of pri, its t not written, a second thing asked for; Budge's numeral 4 is printed before it. m-bꜣḥ 'in the presence (of)' is the sign m (Aa15) and the phallus bꜣḥ (D53) with the roll. Its noun is not written; the presence is that of the lords named after it. ḥr 'at' is the face with its stroke. ḫꜣwt 'altar' is a fan-like plant (coded M12, approximate) for ḫꜣ, t and a stroke, its w not written. nbw mꜣꜥt 'the lords of Maat' is the basket with plural strokes, then the sickle mꜣ crossing the plinth mꜣꜥ, t, the arm ꜥ as complement and the roll with a stroke. The lords of Maat are the gods who sit in judgement over the dead.

sentences.i: coming(?) and going in(?) in the necropolis,
sentences.n: Two words written with the walking legs alone, each a logogram: the first is read ii 'come', the second, whose feet seem to turn the other way in the print, ꜥq 'go in, enter' (Budge: ī, āq). Both readings are Budge's; the signs by themselves show only a verb of motion, so they are doubtful. They are taken as infinitives, more things asked of Osiris. m 'in' is the owl, and ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis' is written as before. To come and go freely, and not be shut in the tomb, is what the dead ask for again and again.

sentences.l: not · being-turned-back · ba-my · seeing(?) · the-Disk · beholding · the-Moon · for-ever · (twice)
sentences.i: without my ba being turned back, seeing(?) the Disk and beholding the Moon for ever. (Twice.)
sentences.n: The papyrus writes šn·tw, without the arm ꜥ; read šnꜥ·tw 'is turned back' (the Hymn to Osiris has the same phrase with the arm). The word is the cord loop šn (coded V7, approximate) with water n as complement, then t and the w (Z7) of the sḏm·tw·f, the passive, negated by n (the arms of negation with n), with the noun bꜣ·i as its subject: 'my ba not being turned back'. bꜣ·i 'my ba' is the jabiru bꜣ with the small censer (R7) at its foot as classifier, and a short stroke for ·i. The next sign is not identified: a small ring with a hooked body and a hatched arc, which matches no known sign; it is coded D4, the eye, only as the nearest sign for 'see'. Budge's reading [maa] 'the sight of', in square brackets in his transliteration only, is a guess from the sense, and it is followed here with a query. mꜣꜣ(?) 'seeing' and dgg 'beholding' are taken as infinitives, more things asked for after di·k n·i in the third line, like pr, ii and ꜥq; Budge instead hangs them on the turning back ('from the sight of'), with a 'from' that is not written. iṯn 'the Disk' is the reed i, the tethering rope ṯ, n and the sun as classifier: the sun's disk, with ṯ for t (Budge: àθen), as in the Hymn to Ra. dgg 'beholding' is a long sign with a cap (coded X4, approximate), the jar-stand g twice and the eye as classifier: the doubled form of dgi 'look, behold', which the Hymn to Ra writes with the hand d. The first sign stands where the hand should be and is read d, but it is doubtful (Budge reads t: teḳeḳ). The papyrus writes iḥ, without the arm ꜥ; read iꜥḥ 'the Moon': the reed i and the wick ḥ, with a seated god wearing the disk and crescent (coded A40, approximate) as classifier, as in the Hymn to Ra; Budge's numeral 5 is printed before it. ḏt 'for ever' is the cobra ḏ, t and the flat land sign (N16, approximate). sp sn, a plain circle over two strokes, tells the reader to say the words twice. To see the sun by day and the moon by night is to share the daily round of the sky.

sentences.i: Said by Sa-mer-ef. He says:
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd·f in red; here, unlike the first section, ḏd in is black (Budge prints no line over it). The third section begins, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1. ḏd in is the cobra with the hand and the reed with water n, as before. The name is a long-necked duck (coded G39, the pintail; it may be G38), sꜣ 'son', with a stroke, then the hoe mr lying over the mouth r, its complement, and the viper f: sꜣ-mr-f, 'the son whom he loves' (Budge: Se-mer-f), with mr·f the relative form of mri 'love'. It has no classifier. Sa-mer-ef, like Iun-mut-ef in the first section, is a title of Horus as the beloved son of Osiris, also borne by the priest who takes the son's part in the rites; the two present Ani in turn.

sentences.i: I have come to you, tribunal who are in Rosetau.
sentences.n: Budge prints ii and ḫr·tn as one group; they are divided here into the verb and the preposition with its suffix. ii 'I have come', without the 'I', and ḫr·tn 'to you' are written as in the first section. ḏꜣḏꜣt 'tribunal' is written as before, with plural strokes after the seated god in place of the single stroke. imyw 'who are in' is the sign im, the chick w and a stroke. rꜣ-sṯꜣw 'Rosetau' is the mouth with its stroke, the drag-rope sṯꜣ (V2, approximate) and the desert-hill sign, here without plural strokes. Where Iun-mut-ef addresses the tribunal of heaven, earth and the necropolis, Sa-mer-ef addresses the tribunal of Rosetau.

sentences.l: grant · bread · water · breath · a-field(?) · in · the-Field-of-Offerings · like · the-followers · of-Horus
sentences.i: Grant bread, water, breath and a field(?) in the Field of Offerings, like the followers of Horus.
sentences.n: imi 'grant' is the reed i, the sign m (Aa15) written twice and the arm, printed flat: the imperative of rdi, as in the first section, here with nouns as its objects. t 'bread' is t with the lidded pot and the loaf as classifiers and a stroke. mw 'water' is the three water lines alone. nfw 'breath, air' is the sail (coded P5, approximate) with w and plural strokes. ꜣḥt 'a field' (?) is two uprights with stays (coded O22, approximate) with two small wedges of land (coded N21, approximate) and a stroke. Budge reads seḥ 'an estate', taking the first sign as the booth sḥ, but sḥ is a booth or hall, not land; as in the same wish in the scene of the weighing of the heart and in the Hymn to Osiris, the word is taken as ꜣḥt 'field', with the land wedges as classifiers. No sign clearly writes ꜣḥ and no t is written, so the reading is doubtful. m 'in' is Aa15. sḫt-ḥtpt 'the Field of Offerings' is three reeds on a base, sḫt, with t, a small wedge and a stroke, then the loaf on a mat ḥtp with t and p as complements (the p printed as an oval, coded Q3), t, a long loaf (coded X4, approximate) and plural strokes: here written with the feminine ḥtpt 'offerings' (Budge: Seχet-ḥetepet). mi 'like' is the milk jug in its net (W19). šmsw 'the followers' is the sign šms (coded T18, approximate) with a stroke; ḥr 'Horus' is the falcon with the seated god. The Field of Offerings is the land of plenty of the blessed dead, and the followers of Horus, the god's company of old, already dwell there.

sentences.i: Hail to you, king of the necropolis, ruler of Igeret!
sentences.n: ind-ḥr·k 'hail to you' is printed as in the second section, with the sign nḏ (coded Aa27, approximate) after the reed; the signs shown are Budge's. His footnote says that the papyrus itself has a second reed where he prints nḏ: the papyrus writes ii ḥr·k (two reeds, the face with its stroke and the basket); read ind-ḥr·k. The greeting is the only sense the place allows; the scribe has dropped or misdrawn its middle sign. nswt 'king' is the sedge plant nsw with t and water n as complement; nswt ẖrt-nṯr 'king of the necropolis' is a direct genitive. ḥqꜣ 'ruler' is the crook ḥqꜣ with a seated figure as classifier (coded A40; the print shows a long-wigged figure without a staff). nw 'of' is the pot nw with a stroke, the genitive adjective in its plural form, here after a singular noun. igrt 'Igeret' is the reed i, the jar-stand g, r, t and the desert-hill sign: the realm of the dead, perhaps 'the silent land' (Budge: Àkert). Osiris rules the dead as a king rules the living.

To know a god's counsels is to be one of his own.

sentences.i: I am equipped with your forms of the Duat.
sentences.n: ꜥpr·kwi 'I am equipped' is the sign ꜥpr (Aa20, a bag on a cord) with the mouth r as complement, the roll with its tie and the basket k: the stative of ꜥpr 'equip, provide', its ending written with k alone, as in rḫ·kwi (Budge supplies [uà]; his numeral 3 is printed before the word). m 'with' is the owl. irw·k 'your forms' is the reed i as complement, the eye ir, r again, a standing mummy (A53) and the roll with a stroke as classifiers, and ·k: irw 'form', its w not written. n 'of' is water n, the genitive. dwꜣt 'the Duat' is the star in a circle (N15) alone. A god's forms are the shapes he can take; to be equipped with them is to be able to take them in the world below.

sentences.l: may-give-you · to-me · a-place · in · the-necropolis · beside · the-lords · of-Maat
sentences.i: May you give me a place in the necropolis beside the lords of Maat,
sentences.n: Budge prints di·k n·i as one group; it is divided here. di·k 'may you give' is the arm with a loaf and ·k, and n·i 'to me' is water n and the seated man, as in the second section. st 'place' is the throne st with t as complement and the house as classifier. m 'in' is the owl; ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis' as before. r-gs 'beside' is the mouth r and a bevelled sign (Aa15) standing for the sign gs, with a stroke; Budge reads erma 'near', taking the sign as m. nbw 'the lords' is the basket with the chick w and a stroke. mꜣꜥt 'Maat', at the head of line 4, is the sickle crossing the plinth, t, and the roll with a stroke; no arm ꜥ is printed.

sentences.i: my field(?) established in the Field of Offerings,
sentences.n: ꜣḥt·i 'my field' (?) is the sign coded O22 (approximate) with the two small wedges and a stroke, read ꜣḥt as in the third section (Budge: seḥ-à), and the seated man ·i. mn 'established, lasting' is the gaming board mn with water n as complement and the roll: the stative after its noun, 'my field (being) established'. m 'in' is Aa15. sḫt-ḥtpw 'the Field of Offerings' is the three reeds with a wedge, a stroke and t, then the loaf on its mat ḥtp, with a long loaf (coded X4, approximate) and plural strokes; this time ḥtp has no t after it.

sentences.i: and may I receive offering loaves before you.
sentences.n: šsp 'receive' is the sign šsp (O42), hatched in the print, with the stool p as complement and the low sign U15 as classifier. No suffix is written, and Budge supplies '[may I]': it is taken as a sḏm·f with its 'I' left out, a wish like di·k. snw 'offering loaves' is the bolt s, water n, the pot nw, the chick w as complement, a long loaf (coded X4, approximate) and plural strokes. m-bꜣḥ·k 'in your presence' is the owl m, the phallus bꜣḥ (D53) and the roll with its tie, then ·k and a stroke. The introduction ends here; the spell proper begins with Plate 13.
